item.title: Silicon Valley is already plotting a comeback for ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
SAN FRANCISCO — A day after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, Silicon Valley is already anticipating his comeback. As a close ally of Donald Trump, regularly taking calls — even publicly — from the president, Huang became one of the most prominent and influential voices in Washington for the largely California-based tech industry, leaving a vacuum with his departure from one of the world’s most profitable companies that has become the backbone of the AI boom. But while national security hawks and tech skeptics in Washington prepare to haul him before Congress to bring further scrutiny of his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, Silicon Valley leaders are mourning his swift exit and positing ways that he could return. The founder of defense tech giant Anduril, Palmer Luckey , and Perplexity AI CEO Aravind Srinivas have rushed to Huang’s defense, while SpaceXSI CEO Elon Musk has even floated the idea of hiring him. Five other tech industry insiders also told POLITICO they expect Huang to eventually return in a major way to leadership within Silicon Valley. Another three were not quite as confident, but indicated they wouldn’t be surprised if it happened. “It is inevitable, with all of the value that he’s created and his role commonly accepted as the godfather of AI, that he will have a second act,” said an executive at a prominent California startup who was granted anonymity to frankly discuss industry dynamics. “And that any number of hyperscalers and startups are tripping over themselves to reach out to him and bring him on, regardless of any transgressions.” Despite losing his lofty perch at Nvidia, Huang still has a net worth of roughly $145 billion , an ecosystem of connections in high places and a sterling entrepreneurial reputation within the industry, some noted. “That kind of influence doesn’t just disappear overnight,” said Joseph Hoefer, chief AI officer at the lobbying firm Monument Advocacy. “I wouldn’t confuse losing his position with losing his ability to shape what comes down the road.” A spokesperson for Huang did not respond to a request for comment on his future plans. Three of the people who spoke with POLITICO said it would be easier for Huang to start a new venture using his wealth of capital, rather than joining an already established company. The connection to allegations of espionage “would make it much harder for any public company to bring him on board in a leadership role,” said Scott Gerber, partner at the tech strategy consultancy Vrge. Others have started to seize on questions about the initial reports of Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, potentially undercutting any support for his ouster. Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), who will likely be the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, told POLITICO this week that he’s unsure whether Huang’s paramour was knowingly providing information to China based on briefings from U.S. intelligence officials. David Sacks, Trump’s former AI czar and a venture capitalist prominent on the tech right, highlighted reports that some in the U.S. intel community have similar doubts. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” he wrote in an X post . Recouping influence in Washington, however, may still be trickier than in Silicon Valley. Huang has been a commanding voice in advocating for looser restrictions on exports to China of advanced semiconductors — necessary for the development of artificial intelligence. That position is being called into question by lawmakers in Congress, given an initial Financial Times report that U.S. intelligence believed Huang was having an affair with a spy. “His standing in industry might be recoverable over time,” said Philip Reiner, CEO of the Institute for Security and Technology think tank in California and a former senior director at the National Security Council. “Rebuilding credibility in Washington on China policy is extremely challenging.” Even still, much of the cachet he built was specifically connected to Trump’s White House, meaning it would have an expiration date regardless, ahead of the 2028 election, others noted. “[M]uch of his political influence was tied to his relationship with the current administration, and that kind of access will be hard to rebuild once the political landscape shifts,” said Nu Wexler, a principal at Four Corners Public Affairs who advises tech companies on policy communications. This delicate position raises the stakes for an upcoming House hearing on the scandal, for which Huang has agreed to testify . “If he can come before Congress and own mistakes, but also explain them and still be a credible voice, that will go a long way towards opening the door for anything else that he would want to do in Washington and the private sector,” said Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation — a think tank funded by Big Tech companies like Amazon and Microsoft. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/13/silicon-valley-plots-jensen-huangs-comeback-01166322

item.title: After 26 years, the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nearly all measles cases have been in people who had not received the highly effective measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. - Jayla Whitfield-Anderson/Reuters Thanks to widespread vaccination, measles had been considered “eliminated” as a continually transmitting illness in the United States since 2000 – but not anymore. An independent commission of experts that reports to the director of the Pan American Health Organization determined that the US no longer qualified as having eliminated measles, a source close to the process told CNN on Friday. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. The decision was widely expected after years of falling vaccination levels and surging case counts, but it’s still a black mark on the nation’s public health policy. The international committee that determines countries’ measles elimination status considers an infection to be endemic, or regularly occurring, if infections caused by the same strain are passed from person to person for at least a year within the same country. To determine this, the committee members look at the genetic code of viruses sampled from patients. Every time a virus copies itself, it makes tiny changes in its genetic code. By studying the genomes of different viruses in an outbreak, scientists can determine how closely the infections may be related and whether they are likely to have been part of the same chains of transmission. In August, scientists with Utah’s public health laboratory published a preprint study showing that the same strain of measles had been circulating in the state for more than a year, accounting for more than 95% of cases there. It traveled from the southwest part of the state to central Utah, ultimately causing more than 600 cases between June 2025 and June 2026. There have also been sustained outbreaks in South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York, as well as other states. It’s not clear what data the committee relied on to make its decision, but it wasn’t exactly a tough call, said Dr. Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the University of Saskatchewan in Canada and Editor-in-Chief of the journal Vaccine. The Utah data alone would have been enough to make the case, she said. The US has logged record numbers of measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths for the past two years, even as some members of the Trump administration – including President Donald Trump – have cast doubt on the safety and effectiveness of the vaccines that prevent it. “Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system. It shows cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is so effective that two doses cut an exposed person’s chances of getting sick by 97% compared with someone who is unvaccinated. Since 2000, when measles was declared eliminated in the United States, the country has still some outbreaks every year. These were touched off by sick travelers who brought the virus into the country. Because of community protection maintained by high vaccination rates, these outbreaks were usually small and short-lived. In 2025 and 2026 , however, the virus found more families and communities that were unvaccinated, leaving them vulnerable to infection. More than 5,400 measles cases have been reported in the US this year – the highest number since 1991. Most are linked to the 43 new outbreaks this year, but more than 1,000 cases are linked to outbreaks that began last year. Nearly all of this year’s cases have been in people who had not received the MMR vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported cases, according to the CDC , and at least 10 people have died after catching measles, according to state reports. ‘Measles is back’ The declaration is a humbling moment for a nation that played a leading role in ridding the world of smallpox – the only human disease to have ever been wiped out worldwide – and worked for decades to drive measles offshore. “This is just so devastating and so sad that we are where we are today,” said Dr. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an infectious disease epidemiologist at Columbia University Irvine Medical Center in New York. “This just kind of points towards the direction of really reversing a generation of public health progress.” But it also means people who are too young to be vaccinated against measles or who have lowered immune function because of organ transplants or cancer or other conditions are at higher risk in areas with outbreaks than they were just two years ago. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported measles cases this year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. - Shannon Stapleton/Reuters Most people who get measles will recover after having a fever and a rash and feeling generally miserable for several days, said Dr. William Moss, a professor and measles expert at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. But that doesn’t mean the infection is benign, he said. Measles can also wipe out a person’s immune memory. The immune system forgets which infections it’s fought off before, leaving the person vulnerable to secondary threats like pneumonia or diarrhea. If a pregnant woman catches measles, she can pass it to her baby in the womb, and the baby will be born with measles, putting its life at risk. In rare cases, people who’ve had measles can develop serious neurologic complications, sometimes years after the original infection. The most serious is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, which is progressive and fatal. All of these complications can be prevented by vaccination. The United States losing its measles elimination status is “incredibly embarrassing,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston. But, he said, it’s a signal of an more important message: “Basically, measles is back.” “Whether or not we’ve officially lost our elimination status to me is much less important than, basically, measles is here. It’s pervasive, and vaccination rates are down across the country, and I don’t see us getting back to normal anytime soon,” he added. Could the US regain its elimination status? Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to science. A single infected person typically spreads it to 12 to 18 others. The virus is airborne and can float in a room for hours after a sick person leaves it. Soon after the measles vaccine was deployed in the early 1960s, public health experts realized that if enough people in an area were vaccinated, the protection from the shot could stop the spread of the virus. The US set its first goal to eliminate measles transmission in 1978. Measles is one of the 30 diseases targeted for elimination by 2030 by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO. In 2016, PAHO and the World Health Organization declared the 35 countries in the Americas region to be free of ongoing measles transmission. That designation was lost last year, however, when Canada’s elimination status ended after a lengthy outbreak that spanned several provinces. Mexico, which has had several large measles outbreaks of its own, is also in danger of losing its elimination status. Moss said that since the US has lost its measles elimination status, it has to be on the path to regaining it. “That’s not easy, particularly in the current environment with diminished public trust in vaccines, the increasing nonmedical exemptions that we’re seeing in schools, and declines in measles, mumps and rubella vaccination among our kindergarten students, and the undermining of vaccine policy,” Moss said. “So it’s not going to be a trivial task for the United States to regain its measles elimination status.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/13/health/us-measles-elimination-status

item.title: Trump's midterm setback leaves some longtime supporters questioning MAGA's future
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
COLUMBUS, Ohio - The young Republicans had grown restless even before their disastrous election, tired of President Donald Trump, his war and his handpicked candidates. Now about a dozen members of Ohio State University College Republicans plopped down their backpacks for their first meeting since the election and pondered what was next. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Abraham Dixon, 20, used to identify with Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement. But MAGA seemed synonymous with loyalty to Trump, and he'd come to think of Trump as "the anchor around the elephant's neck." He worried that even a politically diminished Trump would keep bending the party to his will - and compared him to the aging emperor villain of Star Wars. "He's Palpatine," Dixon said. It was hard to picture the GOP without the man who defined it for a decade. Trump's GOP was all they knew: Many cast their first votes for him. But chapter president Hunter Willmitch was blunt in an interview about the changes underway: "The MAGA movement, in my opinion, is dead." MAGA is certainly muddled, as its rank-and-file voters look to leaders outside of the Trump administration, have crossed over to Democrats or disengaged from politics altogether. There is no consensus about who should run in 2028 and plenty of skepticism for Vice President JD Vance, who once seemed the heir apparent. Like Trump or not, everyone agrees his vacuum will be hard to fill. Right-wing influencers increasingly critical of Trump were declaring themselves vindicated by his rebuke in the midterms. Extremists like Nick Fuentes, the white-supremacist influencer, saw the chaos on the right as an opportunity. "We could not have asked for a better outcome," Fuentes declared on his live stream. It was a moment of both peril and opportunity for the Ohio State College Republicans who held their meeting in an empty classroom one night this week. "How are you?" a young woman asked Willmitch as she sat down. "Upset at the amount of losses we took," Willmitch said. "Tuesday was rough," she said. "I thought it was going to be a little rough," Willmitch echoed. "I just didn't expect … that." He mentioned the bright spot in Florida, where Republicans had weathered the blue wave and Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) was preparing another presidential bid. "If it's not for Ron DeSantis, that [state] probably flips," Willmitch said. He liked what he was hearing from the Florida governor, a longtime champion of the culture wars who now said Republicans needed to stop "fighting yesterday's battle" - prioritizing issues like the rise of artificial intelligence rather than pouring money into ads about transgender issues. Dixon agreed that the party's best bet was someone outside the Trump administration like DeSantis. He snorted when another student brought up Trump's latest interview on "60 Minutes," in which he suggested he wanted to compromise with Democrats on immigration. Republicans were like "a dog under the dinner table," the other student vented, told to be grateful for what Trump handed them. He wanted the party to run more staunch conservatives and talk more about the new populist issues animating both the right and the left: Flock cameras and data centers. Ohio state Rep. Brian Stewart (R), an Ohio State alumnus, was there as a guest speaker and was frank about the party's struggles this election cycle. Yes, Republicans were drawn into fighting old battles, he said, but "part of it too is we didn't have a lot of good things to say." A student asked him what the GOP should look like after Trump, and Stewart said Trump's overhaul of the party would endure in "the way we interact with the media, the way we sort of address questions, the way we sort of take criticism." "There used to be this just this defensive crouch that every Republican officeholder had," Stewart said - no longer. Yet Republicans couldn't just mimic Trump, he warned. The president had long defied political gravity, saying and doing things that other politicians would never get away with. He said other elected officials would need to abide by "a baseline of kindness and respectability." "We need voters to like us." A 'Front Row Joe' packs up Rick Frazier's living room was still plastered with mementos from his decade as one of Trump's "Front Row Joes" who followed him to rallies around the country. There was his picture with Trump, signed in gold pen. There was his photo with another Trump superfan best known as "Brick Suit." There was the framed letter he got from Trump in 2023 after his daughter died of a drug overdose. "Melania and I are devastated," the letter read. Frazier, 70, had thrown himself into the MAGA movement more fervently than almost anyone in the country, hooked from the moment Trump came down a golden escalator in 2015. Retired from a factory that made tank tracks for the military, he believed Trump would "drain the swamp" and help American industry. Now Frazier was done with him. From his couch in western Ohio, he laughed along at an episode of the comedy show "South Park," which has brutally and crudely skewered Trump and his administration over the past year. "He's the king of swamp," he said. Frazier's shift unfolded gradually, he said. He barely spoke about it with the other Front Row Joes - most of whom still adored Trump. He didn't like it when Trump resisted his supporters' push to release the government's full files on the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and he cringed when Trump, from the rally stage, mocked the word "affordability." He voted for Trump to straighten out the southern border and crack down on the drug trade that stole his daughter, and he couldn't make sense of Trump's decision last year to pardon a former Honduran president convicted for overseeing a "narco-state" that routed cocaine to the United States. "See, that got me all upset," he said, his voice wavering. His last Trump rally was in Kentucky, where the president railed against Rep. Thomas Massie (R), a rebellious Republican whom Frazier liked. When the midterms came, Frazier voted for his longtime Republican congressman Jim Jordan but also backed Democrats for governor and Senate, helping to flip Ohio blue. This week, he watched live as Massie unsuccessfully moved to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war with Iran. "I'm kind of going to go back to the way I was before Trump," Frazier said. "I was independently swinging wherever the best guy was running. And that's the way I think it should be. " Frazier still liked Vance, whom he's met, and thought the vice president was being honest about Republicans' missteps. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote on X the day after the midterm elections. But Frazier and plenty of other Trump voters were up for grabs now - and it wasn't clear who could turn him into a Front Row Joe again. 'Nobody worth voting for' At a chicken wing chain in southern Ohio, Heather Romine said she was raised to believe that you can't complain about things if you don't do something about it. So she cast a ballot in every election after she turned 18 - until last week. The 38-year-old conservative voted for Trump, but at some point in his second term, she just stopped following what was happening. "I can't keep up with it," Romine said at the bar, seated next to her boyfriend, who still liked Trump. "I don't want to keep up with it. It's defeating. It feels like it doesn't matter." "There's not a better candidate," her boyfriend said. "Nobody worth voting for," Romine replied. Her rural, working class community in Pike County, Ohio had swung harder to the right in the Trump era than almost anywhere in the country, embodying MAGA's rise. Voters heard Trump's outsider pitch and thought he would be different from other politicians. Now Romine struggled to say what could motivate her to vote again. Republicans won Pike County by a little more than 30 points last week compared to more than 50 points in 2024, in part because people stayed home. "I feel like I'm just a silent person on the sidelines right now, watching the ship burn," Romine said. She voted for Trump because she thought he would "get s--t done," but she felt she got chaos with tariffs and a war that upended the global economy. She owned a house and had a good job in health care, but with three kids, she still felt strained. She could spend $400 on a trip to the grocery store and lost track of how many times she helped buy food over the past year for a friend, a struggling single mother of two. She wanted the country to get back to something more like the "America First" vision Trump pitched - a sentiment others shared. "I think his America First agenda was a good idea, but I don't think he stuck to that," said Brandon Williams, a 46-year-old firefighter who voted three times for Trump. "So I would like to see somebody run somewhere on that same line, but actually do that." Plenty of people in town still supported Trump and thought he was doing the best he could. The war wasn't great, they said, but he closed the borders and pushed back on ideas about gender identity that disturbed them. They were all over the map, however, about who could follow Trump in 2028 and if MAGA would hold together. They were more familiar than most with Vance, an Ohio native who briefly represented the state in the Senate. But they often weren't sure about him and struggled to put their finger on why. "I just don't know, said Rick Patrick, 74, who prefers Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "It's a feeling." Diane Alley, a retired nurse, worried no one could recapture what Trump had stirred up here. "I'm terrified," she said as she made her way through the grocery store. "I don't know who they can run. Nobody is going to equal him." A White House spokesperson pointed to Trump's comments on "60 Minutes" that he thinks MAGA can continue without him. "Because MAGA is basically common sense … strong borders, good military," Trump said. But the president said Republicans would have done better last week if he were on the ballot, "because you saw the level of popularity and love." "There was love," he said. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-gop-knew-now-wonder-172524879.html

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented summit as wars strain global relations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers. While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance. Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump , Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries. Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers. Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran . The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles. Trump does plan on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China . The trilateral meeting is intended to serve as the “beginning of hopefully a conversation” on nuclear disarmament “that can be productive going forward,” said the U.S. official, who added that no agreements are expected to be announced. But Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact. Trump administration officials acknowledge that the nuclear stockpile issue is a difficult one for Beijing to engage on, but the U.S. official characterized the meeting as the moment for China to “step up ... to the adult table” on a matter of international importance. Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige. For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing. “I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like," said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades. More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran. The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University. “You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said. The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years Putin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.” Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi . Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022. As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies. In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine. Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan. Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia , waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war . Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back. Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others. “It’s clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.” ___ Wu reported from Bangkok and Isachenkov from Moscow. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/trump-xi-putin-hold-unprecedented-234022722.html

item.title: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins becomes first Democrat since 1998 elected governor in Alaska
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaska voters have elected a Democrat for governor for the first time since 1998, part of a national midterm elections wave that gave the party sweeping wins in state governments across the country. Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Donald Trump. His victory means Democrats will control the governor's office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control in places such as Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas. Kreiss-Tomkins, often referred to as JKT, completed a political comeback three years after leaving the state House. He traveled throughout Alaska to build his coalition and focused on affordability, advocated for full funding of public schools and called for all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income tax. He also sought a moratorium on new data centers until state lawmakers pass regulations for their development. He said Alaska had become “broken” under eight years of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and needed a change. He cited among other issues a state ferry system that he said has been left in shambles, with routes to many communities cut drastically. The ferry is a key mode of transportation for southeast Alaska communities not connected by roads, some of which also have limited air service. Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents. “If they’re competent, if they’re service-minded, if they’re entrepreneurial, if they’re problem-solvers, you’re on the team. Game on,” he said during a candidate forum last month. “Let’s go, and let’s get Alaska back on track.” Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has at times been at odds with her party, including Trump, endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins a week before the election. She said Kreiss-Tomkins “understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.” Three former governors including Democrat Tony Knowles, independent Bill Walker and Republican Frank Murkowski, the senator’s father, also endorsed him. In a statement declaring victory earlier Friday, Kreiss-Tomkins said voters wanted change and “a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward. Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska.” He said his campaign had more than 10,000 donors. His campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment after The Associated Press called the race. He defeated Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Trump had endorsed Wilson, a business owner, and criticized the other Republican candidates for staying in the race. Bronson is a former mayor of Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, while Taylor was a state attorney general under Dunleavy. Bronson congratulated Kreiss-Tomkins on social media and wished him success. A message seeking comment from Wilson's campaign was not immediately returned. Many Republicans saw ranking as their party’s best shot of retaining the governor's seat. It was a message that conflicted with that of Trump, who has consistently complained about Alaska’s unusual voting method, including during a rally in Alaska in October. Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in August’s open primary, followed by a second Democrat, Tom Begich, who withdrew from the race. Begich’s campaign at the time said it had concluded that the “strongest path to victory is to bring Democratic voters, donors and resources together behind one candidate.” Wilson finished third in the primary. Kreiss-Tomkins said compromise “is a virtue, not a dirty word,” and said he saw the mission of the new governor as working with lawmakers to resolve longstanding problems in the state. The state’s last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving back-to-back terms. Walker served from 2014 to 2018. Kreiss-Tomkins will be sworn in Dec. 7. His lieutenant governor is Zac Johnson, an independent. item.title: Police find credible bomb threat at Illinois plant and urge evacuations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Police in Peoria, Illinois, are investigating a bomb threat at BioUrja Renewables, formerly the ADM plant, and are urging anyone who lives or works within a one-mile radius of the facility to evacuate immediately. The Peoria Police Department said the evacuation recommendation was issued as a precaution while officers and emergency personnel investigated the threat. Police determined at about 6:45 p.m. Friday that a package at the facility was a credible threat and established a one-mile blast radius, officials said. Bomb technicians rendered the package safe at about 9:12 p.m. However, authorities said a thorough search of the large facility was expected to continue into Saturday, likely until late afternoon. Officials said they were not treating the incident as a hoax. "When a bomb threat comes in, typically, it's not legitimate, and they're doing it to cause an evacuation of a building or something like that," Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said at a press conference late Friday. "This is not the case here. We found a credible package that we deem to be a threat. This is ... this is not. We're not considering this a hoax." Authorities have closed most streets in the area and are urging the public to avoid the one-mile radius around the facility until further notice. Residents and businesses within the designated area are being asked to cooperate with emergency personnel and stay away from the area until further notice. "I am actively monitoring the bomb threat in Peoria, and I have directed the Illinois State Police to coordinate with local authorities," Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said in a statement on social media. "Please follow directions from law enforcement and stay clear of the area." Country music singer Jon Pardi's concert in Peoria was also canceled because of its proximity to the bomb threat. Pardi posted a message to his 1 million Instagram followers Friday night, saying, "Peoria, we're disappointed that we won't get to spend tonight with you, but the safety of our fans, our team and the community is always the priority. At the discretion of the Chief of Police, tonight's concert has been canceled due to an active local safety concern. Thank you for your understanding, and stay safe." This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/US/peoria-police-urge-evacuations-after-reported-bomb-threat/story?id=138137440

item.title: Thousands of flights canceled Saturday as airlines struggle to recover from FAA outage
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Airlines across the U.S. worked to recover from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years that canceled more than 2,500 flights Saturday, spread ripple effects around the world, stranded passengers and forced pro and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation. New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said. Airports were slowly returning to normal, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said, with planes taking flight and landing. But the effects could be felt for days, with officials saying the system would likely return to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush. The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023 , when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said the stoppage on Friday had affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day. “The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.” Thousands of flights delayed and canceled At airports across the U.S., passengers stared at screens showing delays or rushed to find buses or trains to their destinations. Emily Brown and her 14-year-old daughter waited more than four hours Friday at the Dallas airport for their flight to Columbus, Ohio, before giving up. They were traveling to surprise her daughter’s best friend. Instead, she had to settle for phoning the friend through tears in the airport, Brown said. “She saved up her money to buy her own ticket, and she’s planned this whole weekend,” Brown said. “Now we’re not sure when we’re gonna be able to go.” A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent greeted passengers at Dallas Love Field at dawn Saturday with “Good morning, good morning,” but then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to expedite the process and help keep flights moving. Sports teams scheduled to play this weekend adjusted game start times, searched for hotel rooms, rescheduled flights and chartered buses. Auburn University's football team opted to take a bus to Mississippi State and the Saturday start time was pushed back from noon ET to 4:15 p.m. Other universities affected by the stoppage included Baylor, Washington, Kansas State, Minnesota and No. 19 Ole Miss, which did not plan to fly until Saturday morning for its game against Oklahoma. More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Corbyn Wascher's flight was on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours Friday on his way home to Moline, Illinois, from a conference in Miami. The 37-year-old high school teacher paid $100 to take an Uber to a hotel 25 minutes from the airport after he was unable to find a flight until Saturday afternoon to Chicago O’Hare International Airport. At London’s Heathrow Airport, several flights to and from the U.S. were listed as delayed or canceled Saturday, including American Airlines flights to Dallas and Los Angeles, and a British Airways flight to New York’s JFK Airport. A Delta flight from Atlanta, an American flight from Miami and a United flight from Chicago were also listed as canceled. “While U.S. flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to rebook affected passengers and get all services back to normal,” said Tim Johnson, consumer director at the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority. Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely Friday. Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He suggested more disruptions might occur. “We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said. “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.” Duffy said the failure Friday involved old equipment and was not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system, which the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky. The problem was due to updating a system that can never shut down, Charlton said. “What you’re watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car’s going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” Charlton said. “It’s a 24/7 operation. And to make changes on the fly, if you’ll pardon that pun, is incredibly complex and dangerous.” The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work. Past problems have been linked to equipment failures The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport . Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots. “If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot. Friday’s ground stop also differed from the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said. ___ Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska, and Golden from Seattle. Associated Press journalists David Keaton in Berlin; Stephen Hawkins in Dallas; Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Jessica Hill in Las Vegas; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Brian Melley in London contributed to this report. item.title: Setback for SpaceX Starship rocket's double-catch test
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Starship rocket launched successfully on Friday [Getty Images] SpaceX will decide later whether to try to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth. The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower. But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch, and instead the booster diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea. The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 1515 local time (2115GMT) on Saturday. This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs. The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 1647 local time (2147GMT) on Friday. The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned. A "go" was initially given by mission control for a catch attempt at the launch tower, but the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding. The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean and burst into flames [Reuters] During a livestream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each manoeuvre safely." The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet. The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off. SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights. But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the "chopsticks". Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space. If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean. A SpaceX lander could take astronauts down to the surface of the Moon [SpaceX] Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX. In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster. Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch. But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society. "Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said. "One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate." After SpaceX became a public company earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will Nasa. The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline. What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next? Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface. But it is not the only company working with Nasa. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touchdown. Both companies will also play a key role in the Artemis III mission, which is currently planned for summer 2027 - another challenging schedule. Four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft will attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers during the voyage. Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended. But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida. Blue Origin had said its spacecraft would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027. Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said the US was in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.
